resources.markdown:
# The dataset

One PostgreSQL database, seven tables, modelling a small e-commerce shop:
customers place orders, orders contain items, items point at products,
products collect reviews, the storefront emits a clickstream of events, and
the company that runs it all has a staff org chart.

Every lesson runs against a throwaway clone of the same template
(`dojo_template`), so you can never break anything permanently. Exact row
counts and distributions live in [dataset_facts.md](dataset_facts.md), which
is regenerated by every `dojo seed` — lesson prose cites numbers from there.

## Relationships

```mermaid
erDiagram
    customers ||--o{ orders : places
    orders ||--o{ order_items : contains
    products ||--o{ order_items : "appears in"
    products ||--o{ reviews : receives
    staff |o--o{ staff : manages
    customers ||..o{ events : "clicks around"
```

(`events.customer_id` is *not* a declared foreign key — clickstreams arrive
too fast to check. That's deliberate, and it matters in Part 5.)

## Tables

### customers — 50,000 rows

| column | type | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| id | int PK | customer id |
| name | text | full name |
| email | text | always `user{id}@example.com` |
| country | text | ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code (`US`, `GB`, ...) |
| created_at | timestamptz | signup time, spread over ~2 years |

### products — 10,000 rows

| column | type | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| id | int PK | product id |
| name | text | e.g. `Nova Kettle 812` |
| category | text | one of: books, electronics, garden, toys, clothing, food |
| price | numeric(10,2) | 1 to 500 |
| description | text | marketing blurb |
| attributes | jsonb | `{"color": ..., "size": ..., "tags": [...]}` — 5 colors, sizes s/m/l/xl, 2 tags |

### orders — 500,000 rows

| column | type | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| id | int PK | order id |
| customer_id | int FK → customers | who ordered (no index! see lesson 33) |
| status | text | pending / paid / shipped / cancelled (paid is ~50%) |
| total | numeric(10,2) | 5 to 2000 |
| created_at | timestamptz | spread over ~1 year |

### order_items — 1,000,000 rows

| column | type | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| id | int PK | line-item id |
| order_id | int FK → orders | parent order |
| product_id | int FK → products | which product |
| quantity | int | 1 to 5 |
| price | numeric(10,2) | unit price at order time (snapshot of the product's price) |

### reviews — 1,000,000 rows

| column | type | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| id | int PK | review id |
| product_id | int FK → products | reviewed product |
| rating | int | 1 to 5 |
| body | text | free text (Part 5 turns this into a full-text search corpus) |
| created_at | timestamptz | spread over ~1 year |

### events — 3,000,000 rows

| column | type | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| id | bigint PK | event id |
| customer_id | int | who (no FK, no index) |
| event_type | text | view / click / add_to_cart / purchase / logout (view dominates) |
| payload | jsonb | `{"path": "/p/<product id>", "value": 0..1000}` |
| ts | timestamptz | **strictly increasing with id** — one event per second. This physical ordering is why BRIN shines here (lesson 43) |

### staff — 500 rows

| column | type | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| id | int PK | employee id |
| name | text | full name |
| department | text | sales / support / engineering / ops / finance |
| manager_id | int FK → staff, NULL for the CEO | reporting line; the org tree is 4 levels deep |
| salary | numeric(10,2) | 40k–250k, higher nearer the top (with deliberate overlaps) |
| hired_on | date | spread over 10 years |

## Things worth knowing before Part 5

- **The template has no indexes beyond primary keys.** Every secondary index
  in this course is one you create yourself.
- Foreign-key columns (`orders.customer_id`, `order_items.order_id`, ...) are
  **not** automatically indexed by PostgreSQL. Lesson 33 turns this into a
  war story.
- The data is deterministic: fixed RNG seed, fixed epoch base, no `now()`.
  Your numbers match this course's numbers, on any machine.

# Further reading

<!-- Generated by tools/gen_further_reading.py - edit the lessons, not this file. -->

Every lesson's `reading.md` ends with a short, specific list of things worth
reading next. This page collects all of them in one place — 201 links across
51 lessons — so you can browse or bookmark without going through the CLI.

To read a lesson's notes with the links in context:

```bash
uv run dojo read <lesson>          # the whole lesson's notes
uv run dojo read <lesson> <exN>    # just the theory behind one problem
```

## The four sources this course leans on

- **[The PostgreSQL manual](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/index.html)** —
  most links below go here. It is unusually well written; the chapters on
  [`EXPLAIN`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/using-explain.html),
  [indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/indexes.html) and
  [routine vacuuming](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/routine-vacuuming.html)
  are worth reading start to finish.
- **[Use The Index, Luke](https://use-the-index-luke.com/)** — Markus Winand's
  free book on indexing and SQL performance. The best single text on the
  subject, and Part 5 refers to it constantly.
- **[Modern SQL](https://modern-sql.com/)** — the same author on the parts of
  SQL that are newer than most people's mental model of it.
- **[Don't Do This](https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Don%27t_Do_This)** — the
  PostgreSQL wiki's list of things that look reasonable and are not. Ten
  minutes, and it will change a schema you were about to write.

## Part 0 — Orientation

### 00_hello_dojo

- [The SQL Language — a first query](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/tutorial-select.html) — the official five-minute version of what you just did.
- [`SELECT` reference page](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html) — dense, and the single most useful page in the docs. Skim it now; you will return to it for the rest of your career.
- [`CREATE DATABASE ... TEMPLATE`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/manage-ag-templatedbs.html) — how `dojo test` gives you a pristine multi-gigabyte database per run.
- [Don't Do This](https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Don%27t_Do_This) — the PostgreSQL wiki's list of things that look reasonable and are not. Worth ten minutes now and another ten after Part 4.

## Part 1 — SQL fundamentals

### 01_select_basics

- [Select Lists](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-select-lists.html) — column labels, `*`, and what `AS` actually binds to.
- [`DISTINCT`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-select.html) — the "Table Expressions" chapter's section on removing duplicate rows; note `DISTINCT ON` waiting at the bottom (lesson 49).
- [Numeric Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-numeric.html) — why money is `numeric` and never `float`. Read the "Arbitrary Precision Numbers" section.
- [Don't Do This — `SELECT *`](https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Don%27t_Do_This) — short, opinionated, and correct.

### 02_where_filtering

- [Comparison Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-comparison.html) — `BETWEEN`, `IN`, `IS DISTINCT FROM`, and the truth tables that make lesson 05 make sense.
- [Pattern Matching](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-matching.html) — `LIKE`, `SIMILAR TO`, and POSIX regexes; note which of them an index can help with.
- [The `WHERE` Clause](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html) — where filtering sits in the logical order of a query's evaluation.
- [Use The Index, Luke — The Where Clause](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/where-clause) — the same clause seen from the index's point of view. You will re-read this in Part 5; skimming it now makes Part 5 easier.

### 03_order_limit

- [Sorting Rows](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-order.html) — `ASC`/`DESC`, `NULLS FIRST`/`LAST`, and what `ORDER BY` can reference.
- [`LIMIT` and `OFFSET`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-limit.html) — including the docs' own warning about inconsistent results without `ORDER BY`.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Paging Through Results](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/partial-results/fetch-next-page) — the definitive explanation of why `OFFSET` is the wrong tool and what keyset pagination looks like.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Top-N Queries](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/partial-results/top-n-queries) — how an index turns `ORDER BY ... LIMIT` into a few page reads. Preview of lesson 35.

### 04_expressions_functions

- [Conditional Expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-conditional.html) — `CASE`, `COALESCE`, `NULLIF`, `GREATEST`, `LEAST`. Short page, high value.
- [String Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-string.html) — `left`, `substring`, `concat`, `format`, and the difference between `||` and `concat()` when an argument is NULL.
- [Mathematical Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-math.html) — including `round`'s two-argument form and what a negative scale does.
- [Type Conversion](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/typeconv.html) — the rules PostgreSQL uses when it *can* infer a cast, and why it refuses to for `||`.

### 05_null_logic

- [Comparison Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-comparison.html) — the truth tables, `IS DISTINCT FROM`, and `IS NULL`. The authoritative source for everything above.
- [`NOT IN` and NULL](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-subquery.html) — the subquery expressions page; read the `NOT IN` paragraph slowly, twice.
- [Don't Do This — NULL handling](https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Don%27t_Do_This) — including why a nullable column with a magic sentinel is worse than a NULL.
- [`NOT NULL` constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/ddl-constraints.html) — the schema-level answer to this entire lesson. Preview of lesson 25.

### 06_aggregates

- [Aggregate Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html) — the complete list, including `bool_and`, `string_agg`, `array_agg`, and the ordered-set aggregates like `percentile_cont`.
- [Aggregate Expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-expressions.html) — the syntax page: where `DISTINCT`, `ORDER BY` and `FILTER` may appear inside an aggregate call.
- [`FILTER`](https://modern-sql.com/feature/filter) — Markus Winand on why `FILTER` replaced `sum(CASE ...)`, with the portability notes.
- [Query Evaluation Order](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html) — the logical order of `FROM`/`WHERE`/`GROUP BY`/`HAVING`, which explains why aggregates cannot appear in `WHERE`.

### 07_group_by_having

- [`GROUP BY` and `HAVING`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html) — the "Table Expressions" chapter, sections 7.2.3 and 7.2.4. Read the functional-dependency paragraph about grouping by a primary key.
- [`SELECT` — the `GROUP BY` clause](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html) — including `GROUP BY` ordinals, output aliases, and a first look at `GROUPING SETS` (lesson 50).
- [`date_trunc` and date/time functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-datetime.html) — the toolkit behind every per-period report. Preview of lesson 18.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Grouping](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/sorting-grouping) — how an index can turn a hash aggregate into a pipelined group aggregate, and why that matters for `LIMIT`.

### 08_inner_joins

- [Joined Tables](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html) — the definitive description of `INNER`/`LEFT`/`RIGHT`/`FULL`, `ON`, `USING`, and `NATURAL`.
- [`SELECT` — FROM clause](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html) — table aliases and how they scope column references.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Joins](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/join) — nested loops, hash joins and sort-merge joins explained from the index outward. This is the best single preparation for lesson 37.
- [Don't Do This — `NATURAL JOIN`](https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Don%27t_Do_This) — why guessing the join key is a bad idea in a schema that will change.

### 09_outer_joins

- [Joined Tables — outer joins](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html) — the formal description of `LEFT`/`RIGHT`/`FULL` and the exact point at which NULL-extension happens relative to `WHERE`.
- [Subquery Expressions — `EXISTS`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-subquery.html) — the other idiomatic anti-join, and why it shrugs off NULLs. Preview of lesson 13.
- [Aggregate Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html) — re-read the `count` entry with outer joins in mind: `count(*)` versus `count(expression)` is the whole of ex3.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Joins](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/join) — why an outer join restricts join-order freedom, and what that costs.

### 10_self_joins_hierarchies

- [Joined Tables and table aliases](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html) — the section on `FROM` items and aliases, which is what makes a self-join legal at all.
- [`WITH` Queries — recursive](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-with.html) — where fixed-depth self-joins stop and lesson 14 begins. Read the org-chart example.
- [Window Functions Tutorial](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/tutorial-window.html) — the other escape from "compare a row to its neighbours". Preview of lesson 15.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Joins](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/join) — why a self-join on an unindexed column is quadratic, and what an index on `manager_id` would change.

### 11_set_operations

- [Combining Queries](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-union.html) — `UNION`, `INTERSECT`, `EXCEPT`, their `ALL` variants, and the precedence rules.
- [`SELECT` — the `UNION`/`INTERSECT`/`EXCEPT` clauses](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html) — the reference-page detail on column matching and where `ORDER BY` may appear.
- [Subquery Expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-subquery.html) — `EXISTS`, `IN`, `ANY`/`ALL`: the other way to express membership, with different NULL and performance behaviour. Preview of lesson 13.
- [Sorting Rows](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-order.html) — why `ORDER BY` after a set operation sorts the whole result and how to sort one branch.

### 12_fundamentals_capstone

- [Date/Time Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-datetime.html) — `date_trunc`, intervals, and the comparison rules that make half-open ranges work. Preview of lesson 18.
- [`generate_series`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-srf.html) — how to produce the periods that `GROUP BY` cannot invent, so an empty month shows as zero.
- [Query Evaluation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html) — worth one more read now that you have used every clause in it.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Top-N Queries](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/partial-results/top-n-queries) — what ex6's `ORDER BY ... LIMIT 5` costs today, and what Part 5 will do about it.

## Part 2 — Intermediate querying

### 13_subqueries

- [Subquery Expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-subquery.html) — `EXISTS`, `IN`, `NOT IN`, `ANY`/`SOME`, `ALL`, and the row-constructor forms. The NULL notes here are the whole of lesson 05 restated.
- [Table Expressions — subqueries in FROM](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html) — derived tables, why they need an alias, and how `LATERAL` lifts the restriction on referring to earlier FROM items (lesson 48).
- [Scalar Subqueries](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-expressions.html) — the one-row-one-column rule and where such a subquery may appear.
- [`WITH` Queries](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-with.html) — the same power with names attached, plus the inlining rules that matter for performance. Lesson 14.

### 14_ctes

- [`WITH` Queries (CTEs)](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-with.html) — the definitive page. Read the recursive section, the cycle-detection example, and the `MATERIALIZED` notes.
- [`SELECT` — `WITH` clause](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html) — the restrictions on where the recursive self-reference may appear.
- [Set Returning Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-srf.html) — `generate_series` for numbers and timestamps: the practical alternative to ex5, and the tool for filling gaps in a time series.

### 15_window_functions_1

- [Window Functions Tutorial](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/tutorial-window.html) — the gentlest correct introduction, with the evaluation-order rules that explain why you cannot filter in `WHERE`.
- [Window Function Calls](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-expressions.html) — the syntax: `PARTITION BY`, `ORDER BY`, frames, and the `WINDOW` clause.
- [Window Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-window.html) — the built-in list: `row_number`, `rank`, `dense_rank`, `ntile`, `lag`, `lead`, `first_value`, `nth_value`.
- [`SELECT` — `DISTINCT ON`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html) — PostgreSQL's shortcut for the N = 1 case of ex6. Lesson 49 makes it a whole topic.

### 16_window_functions_2

- [Window Function Calls — frames](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-expressions.html) — `ROWS`/`RANGE`/`GROUPS`, the default frame, and the exclusion clauses. The most important page in this lesson.
- [Window Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-window.html) — `lag`, `lead`, `first_value`, `last_value`, `nth_value`, `ntile`, `percent_rank`, `cume_dist`.
- [Window Functions Tutorial](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/tutorial-window.html) — worth a second read now that frames make sense.
- [Date/Time Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-datetime.html) — `date_trunc` and interval arithmetic, which every one of these exercises leans on. Lesson 18 next.

### 17_conditional_pivots

- [Aggregate Expressions — `FILTER`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-expressions.html) — the syntax and where `FILTER` may appear.
- [`FILTER` versus `CASE`](https://modern-sql.com/feature/filter) — Markus Winand on the empty-set difference and portability.
- [`tablefunc` / `crosstab()`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/tablefunc.html) — PostgreSQL's actual pivot function, and why its fixed column list is a real constraint.
- [Table Expressions — `LATERAL`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html) — the unpivot idiom's engine. Lesson 48.

### 18_dates_times

- [Date/Time Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-datetime.html) — `date_trunc`, `extract`, `age`, `AT TIME ZONE`, and the interval arithmetic rules. The `date_trunc` week note is in here.
- [Date/Time Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-datetime.html) — the `timestamptz` versus `timestamp` argument, with the storage details that settle it.
- [Set Returning Functions — `generate_series`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-srf.html) — including the timestamp-stepping form used by the gap-days pattern.
- [Don't Do This — timestamp without time zone](https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Don%27t_Do_This) — the short version of the argument, from the PostgreSQL wiki.

### 19_text_jsonb

- [JSON Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-json.html) — `json` versus `jsonb`, the containment semantics, and the indexing section that lesson 42 builds on.
- [JSON Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-json.html) — `->`, `->>`, `#>`, `@>`, `?`, `jsonb_array_elements_text`, and the SQL/JSON path language.
- [String Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-string.html) — `split_part`, `position`, `substring`, `format`, and the regex family.
- [Pattern Matching](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-matching.html) — `LIKE`, `SIMILAR TO`, POSIX regexes, and the note on which of them an index can serve.

### 20_querying_capstone

- [Aggregate Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html) — worth a final pass now that you have used `FILTER`, `DISTINCT` and ordered-set aggregates in anger.
- [`WITH` Queries](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-with.html) — re-read the inlining notes; every query in this lesson is a CTE pipeline.
- [Window Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-window.html) — the reference you will keep open for the rest of your career.
- [Use The Index, Luke](https://use-the-index-luke.com/) — start reading it now. Everything you wrote in Part 2 reads whole tables, and Part 5 is about to explain what that costs and how to stop.

## Part 3 — Modifying data and transactions

### 21_insert_update_delete

- [`INSERT`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-insert.html) — `VALUES`, `INSERT ... SELECT`, `RETURNING`, and `ON CONFLICT` (lesson 22).
- [`UPDATE`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-update.html) — the `FROM` clause and the explicit warning about non-deterministic results when the joined table matches more than once.
- [`DELETE`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-delete.html) — `USING`, `RETURNING`, and the note on `TRUNCATE` as the faster alternative when you mean "all of them".
- [`RETURNING` data from modified rows](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/dml-returning.html) — short, and it will change how you write application code.

### 22_upsert

- [`INSERT ... ON CONFLICT`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-insert.html) — the conflict target rules, `EXCLUDED`, and the notes on which index gets used as the arbiter.
- [`MERGE`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-merge.html) — the SQL-standard alternative from PostgreSQL 15, with its concurrency caveat spelled out.
- [Unique Constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/ddl-constraints.html) — the constraint that makes upsert possible. Lesson 25 designs them.
- [Transaction Isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/transaction-iso.html) — what "atomically" actually means here, and what else races look like. Lesson 23 next.

### 23_transactions

- [Transactions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/tutorial-transactions.html) — the tutorial chapter, including savepoints. Short and worth reading start to finish.
- [Transaction Isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/transaction-iso.html) — read-committed, repeatable-read and serializable, with the anomalies each one permits. The most important page in this lesson.
- [`SAVEPOINT`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-savepoint.html) — the reference page, plus `RELEASE SAVEPOINT` which you will want for long loops.
- [Explicit Locking](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/explicit-locking.html) — `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` and friends, for when read-then-write must not race.

## Part 4 — Schema design and modeling

### 24_ddl_and_types

- [Data Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype.html) — the whole chapter is worth a skim once; the numeric and date/time sections are worth reading properly.
- [`CREATE TABLE`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-createtable.html) — identity columns, generated columns, and the exact syntax for inline constraints.
- [Generated Columns](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/ddl-generated-columns.html) — short page, and it lists the restrictions (immutable expressions, same row only).
- [Don't Do This](https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Don%27t_Do_This) — the type section covers `char(n)`, `varchar(n)`, `money`, `timestamp`, and `serial`. Read it now that you have opinions.

### 25_constraints

- [Constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/ddl-constraints.html) — `NOT NULL`, `CHECK`, `UNIQUE`, primary keys, foreign keys, and `EXCLUDE`. The `ON DELETE` table is in here.
- [`CREATE TABLE`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-createtable.html) — inline versus table-level constraint syntax, and `UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT`.
- [`ALTER TABLE`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-altertable.html) — adding constraints to a table that already has data, including `NOT VALID`. Lesson 28.
- [Index Types — GiST and exclusion constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/rangetypes.html) — the range-type page, which shows the non-overlapping-bookings `EXCLUDE` constraint in full.

### 26_normalization

- [Constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/ddl-constraints.html) — the mechanical half of everything above; normalization without foreign keys is just filing.
- [`ALTER TABLE`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-altertable.html) — `ADD FOREIGN KEY`, `DROP COLUMN`, and what each one locks. Lesson 28 next.
- [Database Design — Normalization (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Database_normalization) — the formal definitions, if you want the normal forms stated precisely rather than as a slogan.
- [Don't Do This](https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Don%27t_Do_This) — read the "Database Encoding" and column-type sections again with a designer's eye.

### 27_views

- [`CREATE VIEW`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-createview.html) — including updatable views, `WITH CHECK OPTION`, and `SECURITY INVOKER`.
- [The Rule System — views](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/rules-views.html) — how PostgreSQL actually implements views by query rewriting. Explains why a view costs what its query costs.
- [`CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-creatematerializedview.html) — the version that stores results, with `REFRESH ... CONCURRENTLY`. Lesson 46.
- [Row Security Policies](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/ddl-rowsecurity.html) — the modern alternative to permission-shaped views.

### 28_altering_live_schemas

- [`ALTER TABLE`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-altertable.html) — the reference page, including the "Notes" section that lists exactly which forms require a rewrite.
- [Explicit Locking — lock modes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/explicit-locking.html) — the conflict matrix. `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` against everything is the row that matters.
- [`CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-createindex.html) — the two-pass build, its restrictions, and what an `INVALID` index means.
- [Routine Vacuuming](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/routine-vacuuming.html) — why dropped columns and updated rows keep their space, and what reclaims it. Lesson 44.

### 29_design_capstone

- [Constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/ddl-constraints.html) — one more pass, now with a design brief in hand.
- [`CREATE VIEW`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-createview.html) — the derived-value half of this lesson.
- [Triggers](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/triggers.html) — where rules go when a CHECK cannot express them. Read the section on constraint triggers.
- [Using EXPLAIN](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/using-explain.html) — start here before lesson 30. Everything you have designed is about to be measured.

## Part 5 — Performance and indexing

### 30_reading_explain

- [Using `EXPLAIN`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/using-explain.html) — the canonical walkthrough, with worked examples of every node type above. Read it once properly; it is the best-written chapter in the manual.
- [`EXPLAIN`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-explain.html) — the options: `ANALYZE`, `BUFFERS`, `VERBOSE`, `SETTINGS`, `FORMAT JSON`.
- [explain.depesz.com](https://explain.depesz.com/) — paste a plan, get the per-node exclusive time and the estimate/actual ratios highlighted. The fastest way to find the guilty node in a large plan.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Anatomy of an Index](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/anatomy) — what a B-tree actually is, which makes every plan node in Part 5 easier to reason about.

### 31_first_index

- [Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/indexes.html) — the whole chapter; start with "Introduction" and "Index Types".
- [`CREATE INDEX`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-createindex.html) — the syntax, including `CONCURRENTLY`, `INCLUDE`, and partial-index predicates.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Anatomy of an Index](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/anatomy) — the clearest explanation anywhere of what a B-tree is and why the leaf nodes are a doubly linked list.
- [Monitoring index usage](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/monitoring-stats.html) — `pg_stat_user_indexes`, for finding the indexes nobody has ever used.

### 32_composite_indexes

- [Multicolumn Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/indexes-multicolumn.html) — the official statement of the prefix rule, and the note on when PostgreSQL will use a non-leading column anyway (badly).
- [Combining Multiple Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/indexes-bitmap-scans.html) — what happens when you have two single-column indexes instead of one composite. Lesson 38.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Concatenated Keys](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/where-clause/the-equals-operator/concatenated-keys) — the phone-book explanation, with diagrams. Read this one.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Ranges](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/where-clause/searching-for-ranges) — why exactly one range column can be used, and why it must be last.

### 33_left_prefix

- [Multicolumn Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/indexes-multicolumn.html) — the prefix rule as the manual states it, including when a non-leading column is used anyway.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Concatenated Keys](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/where-clause/the-equals-operator/concatenated-keys) — the definitive treatment, with the phone-book analogy and the redundant-index argument.
- [`ALTER TABLE ... ADD FOREIGN KEY`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-altertable.html) — and the manual's note that an index on the referencing column is *not* created automatically.
- [Index maintenance](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/monitoring-stats.html) — `pg_stat_user_indexes` for finding both the unused indexes and the redundant prefixes.

### 34_index_only_scans

- [Index-Only Scans and Covering Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/indexes-index-only-scans.html) — the manual's own treatment, including the visibility-map explanation and `INCLUDE`.
- [Routine Vacuuming — the visibility map](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/routine-vacuuming.html) — why an under-vacuumed table cannot do index-only scans. Lesson 44.
- [`CREATE INDEX` — `INCLUDE`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-createindex.html) — the syntax and the restrictions on included columns.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Index-Only Scan](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/clustering/index-only-scan-covering-index) — the same idea from the "clustering data" angle, with the cost model spelled out.

### 35_order_by_and_indexes

- [Indexes and `ORDER BY`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/indexes-ordering.html) — direction, `NULLS FIRST`/`LAST`, and when an ordered scan beats a sort.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Indexing Order By](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/sorting-grouping/order-by) — including the pipelined-order-by argument that makes `LIMIT` cheap.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Paging Through Results](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/partial-results/fetch-next-page) — keyset pagination, now that you have the index that makes it work.
- [`CREATE INDEX`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-createindex.html) — the `ASC`/`DESC`/`NULLS` clauses on index columns.

### 36_statistics_and_the_planner

- [Statistics Used by the Planner](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/planner-stats.html) — what `pg_stats` holds, and how each column is used.
- [Planner Cost Constants](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/runtime-config-query.html) — `random_page_cost`, `seq_page_cost`, `effective_cache_size`. Read the `random_page_cost` note about SSDs.
- [`ANALYZE`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-analyze.html) — sampling behaviour and the per-column statistics target.

### 37_join_algorithms

- [Planner Method Configuration](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/runtime-config-query.html) — the `enable_*` flags, and the manual's warning about using them in production.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Joins](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/join) — nested loops, hash joins and sort-merge joins, each explained from the index outward.
- [Controlling the Planner with Explicit `JOIN` Clauses](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/explicit-joins.html) — `join_collapse_limit`, `from_collapse_limit`, and how to pin a join order when you truly must.
- [Using `EXPLAIN`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/using-explain.html) — re-read the join examples now that the three algorithms have names.

### 38_bitmap_scans

- [Combining Multiple Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/indexes-bitmap-scans.html) — `BitmapAnd`/`BitmapOr` and the manual's advice on single-column versus composite.
- [Using `EXPLAIN`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/using-explain.html) — the bitmap-scan example, including `Heap Blocks` and the recheck line.
- [Resource Consumption — `work_mem`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/runtime-config-resource.html) — the setting that decides when a bitmap goes lossy.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Clustering Data](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/clustering) — why physical order matters so much to the cost of fetching rows.

### 39_partial_indexes

- [Partial Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/indexes-partial.html) — the manual's chapter, including the partial-uniqueness example and the note on predicate proving.
- [`CREATE INDEX`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-createindex.html) — where the `WHERE` clause goes and what expressions it may contain.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Partial Indexes](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/where-clause/null/partial-index) — the NULL-excluding case, explained well.
- [Monitoring index usage](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/monitoring-stats.html) — `pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan`, for confirming your partial index is actually being chosen.

### 40_expression_indexes

- [Indexes on Expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/indexes-expressional.html) — the syntax, the double parentheses, and the cost warning.
- [Function Volatility](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/xfunc-volatility.html) — `IMMUTABLE` versus `STABLE` versus `VOLATILE`, and why only the first can be indexed.
- [Generated Columns](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/ddl-generated-columns.html) — the store-it-instead alternative, with its own trade-offs.
- [JSON Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-json.html) — for ex4's extraction operators; lesson 42 indexes the same column a completely different way.

### 41_gin_fulltext

- [Full Text Search](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/textsearch.html) — the whole chapter. Read the "Controlling Text Search" section for the three query-builders and `ts_rank`.
- [Text Search Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/textsearch-indexes.html) — GIN versus GiST, build cost, and the `fastupdate` behaviour.
- [GIN Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/gin.html) — what an inverted index actually stores, and the pending-list mechanism.
- [`pg_trgm`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/pgtrgm.html) — trigram indexes, for the substring and fuzzy-match cases that full-text search does not cover.

### 42_gin_jsonb

- [JSON Types — `jsonb` Indexing](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-json.html) — the containment semantics and the two operator classes, with size comparisons.
- [JSON Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-json.html) — `@>`, `?`, `#>`, and the SQL/JSON path operators `@?` and `@@`.
- [GIN Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/gin.html) — the inverted-index internals, operator classes, and `fastupdate`.
- [Indexes on Expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/indexes-expressional.html) — the complementary approach from lesson 40; most real schemas want both.

### 43_gist_brin

- [BRIN Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/brin.html) — how block-range summaries work, `pages_per_range`, `autosummarize`, and the operator classes.
- [GiST Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/gist.html) — the extensible framework, its operators, and the k-nearest-neighbour support.
- [Range Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/rangetypes.html) — the `EXCLUDE USING gist` non-overlap constraint, in full.
- [Index Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/indexes-types.html) — the one-page summary of B-tree, hash, GiST, SP-GiST, GIN and BRIN, and what each can answer.

### 44_mvcc_vacuum_bloat

- [Routine Vacuuming](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/routine-vacuuming.html) — dead tuples, the visibility map, freezing, and transaction-id wraparound. The most operationally important chapter in the manual.
- [Concurrency Control (MVCC)](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/mvcc.html) — why readers never block writers, and what a snapshot is.
- [`VACUUM`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-vacuum.html) and [`REINDEX`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-reindex.html) — the options, including `CONCURRENTLY` and what it does not lock.
- [Monitoring Statistics](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/monitoring-stats.html) — `pg_stat_user_tables`, for `n_dead_tup` and the last-vacuum timestamps.

### 45_partitioning

- [Table Partitioning](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/ddl-partitioning.html) — declarative partitioning, pruning, and the "Best Practices" section at the end. Read that section twice.
- [`ALTER TABLE ... ATTACH/DETACH PARTITION`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-altertable.html) — including `CONCURRENTLY` and the locking each form takes.
- [`CREATE TABLE ... PARTITION BY`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-createtable.html) — `RANGE`, `LIST` and `HASH`, and the rules for primary keys on partitioned tables.
- [pg_partman](https://github.com/pgpartman/pg_partman) — the extension most production systems use to create and retire partitions on a schedule.

### 46_materialized_views

- [Materialized Views](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/rules-materializedviews.html) — the concept chapter, with the staleness discussion.
- [`REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-refreshmaterializedview.html) — `CONCURRENTLY`, its unique-index requirement, and `WITH NO DATA`.
- [`CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-creatematerializedview.html) — storage parameters and tablespaces.
- [pg_cron](https://github.com/citusdata/pg_cron) — the usual answer to "what refreshes it", running inside PostgreSQL itself.

## Part 6 — Capstone

### 47_capstone

- [Performance Tips](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/performance-tips.html) — the manual's own summary chapter, worth reading now that every section of it means something to you.
- [Using `EXPLAIN`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/using-explain.html) — one more pass; you will read it differently now than you did in lesson 30.
- [`ALTER TABLE` — Notes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-altertable.html) — the table of which forms rewrite and which do not. Bookmark it.
- [Use The Index, Luke](https://use-the-index-luke.com/) — the whole book, if you have not already. It is the best single text on the subject and it is free.

## Part 7 — Advanced patterns (bonus)

### 48_lateral_joins

- [`LATERAL` Subqueries](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html) — the "Table Expressions" chapter's `LATERAL` section, including the implicit-lateral rule for function calls.
- [`SELECT` — `FROM` clause](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html) — where `LATERAL` may appear and how it interacts with join types.
- [Window Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-window.html) — the other top-N-per-group tool, for the comparison in the notes.
- [Set Returning Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-srf.html) — `unnest`, `generate_series`, `jsonb_array_elements`: the functions most often used laterally.

### 49_distinct_on

- [`SELECT` — `DISTINCT ON`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html) — the reference text, including the warning about unpredictable results without a full `ORDER BY`.
- [Window Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-window.html) — `row_number()`, the portable equivalent.
- [`LATERAL` Subqueries](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html) — the generalisation to N > 1. Lesson 48.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Top-N Queries](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/partial-results/top-n-queries) — the index shape that makes all three approaches fast.

### 50_grouping_sets

- [`GROUPING SETS`, `CUBE`, `ROLLUP`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html) — the "Table Expressions" chapter's section, with the equivalence to `UNION ALL` spelled out.
- [`GROUPING()`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html) — the grouping operations table, for disambiguating subtotal NULLs.
- [`SELECT` — `GROUP BY`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html) — the full grammar, including how grouping sets combine when you list several.

# Interview prep, across every track

Every track in this dojo ends the same way: an **interview part** built for
mid-level full-stack SWE interviews. It is not a separate product — it is the
last part of each course, graded by the same gates, fed into the same
spaced-review scheduler, and honest in the same way (nothing multiple-choice,
nothing autocompleted).

## Where it lives

| track | lessons |
|---|---|
| SQL | `lessons/53_interview_concepts`, `lessons/54_interview_drills` (Part 9) |
| TypeScript | `tracks/typescript/lessons/i1_interview_concepts`, `i2_interview_drills`, `i3_interview_rapidfire` |
| Node | `tracks/node/lessons/i1_…`, `i2_…`, `i3_…` |
| React | `tracks/react/lessons/i1_…`, `i2_…`, `i3_…` |
| C# | `tracks/csharp/lessons/i1_…`, `i2_…`, `i3_…` |
| ASP.NET Core | `tracks/dotnet/lessons/i1_…`, `i2_…`, `i3_…` |

## The three pieces

**1. The question bank (`i1_interview_concepts`).** Each track's bank lives in
that lesson's `reading.md`: 50+ questions with model answers, grouped by
topic, each tagged by how often it actually comes up:

- ⭐⭐⭐ — asked in most interviews for this stack. Know these cold.
- ⭐⭐ — common; expect at least a few.
- ⭐ — differentiators; the questions that separate "pass" from "strong hire".

(The C# track writes these as `[*]`–`[***]` — same scale.)

Answers are written the way a strong candidate would say them out loud — a few
sentences, one concrete example, and the classic follow-up named so it never
surprises you. Every question cross-references the lesson that teaches it:
weak on an answer means redo that lesson, not reread the answer.

How to self-test: open the reading (`dojo read <track> i1_interview_concepts`),
cover each answer, say yours out loud, then compare. Saying it out loud is the
exercise — recognizing a good answer is easy, producing one is the skill.

**2. The drills (`i2_interview_drills`).** Graded exercises written the way an
interviewer would actually phrase them, with a suggested time-box. Treat the
time-box as real: set a timer, no hints on the first attempt. These replicate
the classic hands-on screens for each stack (top-N-per-group in SQL, the
stale-closure counter in React, implement-a-typed-utility in TypeScript,
event-loop output prediction in Node, fix-the-async-bug in C#, the captive
dependency in ASP.NET Core). Each track's challenge exercise is a realistic
45-minute composite task.

**3. Rapid-fire + spaced repetition (`i3_interview_rapidfire`).** The ⭐⭐⭐
concepts appear *again* as fresh exercises, and every interview lesson ships a
review variant wired into the dojo's ten-stage spaced-review ladder (3 → 7 → 21 → 60 → 120 → 240 → 365 → 540 → 730 → 1,095
days). This is deliberate: the highest-frequency interview material is exactly
the material worth over-learning, and the ladder does the repetition for you.
Run `dojo review` when it tells you something is due — that is the whole
system.

## A schedule that works

- **Learning phase:** finish a track's numbered lessons before its interview
  part. The drills assume the course.
- **Maintenance phase:** `dojo review` daily (it is usually empty; when it
  isn't, it is short). This keeps every track's ⭐⭐⭐ set warm indefinitely.
- **Two weeks before interviewing:** redo `i2_interview_drills` for your
  target stack under real time-boxes, and read the full `i1` bank for every
  track the role touches. `dojo status` shows where you are weakest — the
  lessons with the most attempts and hints are the ones to redo.
